items.gist: Kalā is not the principal instrument; it prompts inert agency, while consciousness is not strengthened by Īśa's power alone.
Distinguishing māyā and puruṣa prevents descent below māyā; Sāṃkhya-style pradhāna descent is rejected.
Seeing the self free from mala leads to Śivahood; kalā is distinct and not one universal world.
Partial agency is broken into limited knowledge; vidyā discriminates experiences and buddhi is mixed with guṇas.
The reflected object is not merely external light; buddhi-gata bhāva falls within vidyā's instrumentality.
Rāga, vidyā, niyati, and kāla form kalā's work, culminating in bhoktṛ-bhāva.
Māyā, kalā, rāga, vidyā, kāla, and niyati are the six kañcukas; kalā is subtle and smooth.
Vidyā discriminates pleasure and pain; rāga arises like dye, binding the paśu in enjoyment.
Kalā produces both bhoktṛ and bhogya together; their mutual distinction and dissolution are explained.
Kalā produces rāga and vidyā together; the apparent sequence is denied at the level of thinghood.
Experienced objects are reduced to guṇas; disturbed guṇas produce effects and bhuvana is shown distinctly.
Īśvara's will agitates prakṛti for bhoktṛtva; buddhi tattva arises pure and receives reflection.
Ahaṃkāra arises in buddhi; fivefold vāyu sustains life, and the instrument aggregate is threefold.
Sattva-predominant ahaṃkāra yields manas, buddhi, and senses; manas is the all-object faculty.
Prāṇa is not an inner instrument due to inertness; avasāya, abhimāna, and kalpanā are not action, and ahaṃkāra becomes the auditory instrument.
